claim: China installed roughly 295,000 industrial robots in 2024, about 54% of global installations
caveat: Installations measure deployment activity, not realized productivity
notes: Verified against IFR press materials 2026-07-05

claim: China's operational industrial robot stock exceeds 2 million units, the largest in the world
caveat: Aggregate stock reflects economy size as well as automation intensity

claim: IFR World Robotics 2025 revised China's manufacturing robot density to 166 per 10,000 employees (22nd worldwide) after incorporating updated National Bureau of Statistics workforce data; the United States stands at 307 (8th); South Korea leads at 1,220; the global average is 132
caveat: Density is highly denominator-sensitive: IFR's prior releases showed China at 470 per 10k for 2023 under the old workforce series. Cross-year density comparisons must state which denominator is used
notes: Verified against live IFR press page 2026-07-05. Supersedes any use of 470 or 567 figures for China density

claim: China's robot deployment is clustered in coastal hubs and subsidized strategic sectors, while a long tail of interior SMEs remains labor-dependent
caveat: Interpretation inferred from the density revision plus academic digital-divide evidence; no direct plant-level dataset yet
notes: Consistent with the 166-vs-aggregate-stock contrast but not directly measured

claim: Chinese robot makers took a majority share (~57%) of their domestic market for the first time in 2024
caveat: Figure appears in IFR press materials but was not independently re-verified on 2026-07-05
notes: VERIFY against WR2025 press release before public use

claim: The August 2025 State Council AI+ opinion (Guofa [2025] No. 11) sets application-penetration targets for new-generation smart terminals and agents of over 70% by 2027 and over 90% by 2030
caveat: This is a stated policy target, not an observed adoption statistic
notes: Primary State Council document is canonical src-0023

claim: Chinese AI policy since 2024 is primarily a diffusion program (AI+ across industry, science, services, governance) rather than a frontier-model program
caveat: Characterization of policy intent; implementation and outcomes are separate questions. China also invests in frontier capability
notes: Core China conversion hypothesis; treat as testable

claim: The 15th Five-Year Plan elevates digital-intelligent development to a standalone chapter and schedules landmark compute-infrastructure projects
caveat: Official statement of plan structure; staged source pending URL verification
notes: Promote src-v1-dr-018 before using in public copy

claim: CAICT reports China's smart compute reached 782 EFlops by mid-2025, about 81% of total domestic compute
caveat: CAICT is MIIT-affiliated; treat scale figures as official-adjacent claims, not independently validated
notes: Staged pending URL verification

claim: Independent Chinese academic work finds only ~2% of surveyed manufacturing firms achieve comprehensive digital reinvention, with an initial productivity dip during AI integration
caveat: Single study; sample limited to listed companies; needs journal DOI for canonical promotion
notes: Strongest independent counterweight to official diffusion claims

claim: Converting AI investment into TFP gains in Chinese firms requires shedding routine labor while adding non-routine high-skill labor, cutting against social-stability mandates
caveat: Working paper; URL incomplete in staged research; verify before public use
notes: Mechanism evidence for adaptation-stress pillar

claim: MOHRSS is preparing a dedicated policy document on coping with AI's employment impact, alongside subsidized retraining programs
caveat: Media relay of ministry statement; primary document not yet located
notes: Signal that Beijing anticipates AI-driven labor friction

claim: The US AI Action Plan states the bottleneck to capturing AI's benefits is not model availability but slow adoption inside large organizations and critical sectors
caveat: Official framing by the White House; itself a claim about the economy, not a measured outcome

claim: US grid interconnection queues stretch to multiple years, and NERC reliability assessments flag data-center-driven load growth as an emerging risk
caveat: Queue duration varies by region; NERC assessments are forward-looking risk statements

claim: FERC Orders 2023 and 1920 are active federal reforms aimed at interconnection and regional transmission bottlenecks
caveat: Reform adopted is not reform delivered; implementation timelines run to the 2030s

claim: Federal AI adoption is an explicit US policy channel via OMB M-25-21/M-25-22 and agency adoption strategies
caveat: Procurement intent, not demonstrated demand at scale yet

claim: Across OECD countries about 20% of firms report using AI, roughly doubling from 8.7% two years earlier, with large firms adopting at ~3x the rate of small firms
caveat: Extensive-margin measure; survey definitions differ across agencies
notes: Figures consistent across Eurostat and OECD releases; promote sources before public use

claim: Over 70% of euro-area firms report some AI use but only about 7% use it intensively (ECB SAFE Q4 2025)
caveat: Intensity self-reported; euro-area only
notes: The depth-deficit anchor claim; promote src-v1-dr-005 before public use

claim: US adoption figures diverge sharply by weighting: 17-20% firm-weighted (Census BTOS) versus ~78% employment-weighted exposure (Fed SBU)
caveat: Different surveys, definitions, and respondent pools; a weighting artifact, not a contradiction
notes: Median firm is a non-adopter; median worker is at an adopting firm

claim: IMF modeling projects Europe's medium-term TFP gain from AI at roughly 1% cumulative over five years; OECD projects +0.4-1.3pp annual labor-productivity growth over ten years in high-exposure G7 economies
caveat: Model estimates, not observed outcomes; ranges depend on adoption and regulation assumptions
notes: Keep projected and observed gains visually separate in product

claim: Computing infrastructure reached roughly 1.5% of US GDP in Q1 2026 (AI-specific ~0.8%), making the buildout channel the dominant near-term macroeconomic effect of AI
caveat: Epoch trend-decomposition estimate, not an official BEA line item
notes: Supports the essay's investment-before-payoff argument

claim: AI's current GDP footprint runs mostly through investment and some government spending, not consumption or exports; it measures the size of the bet, not the payoff
caveat: Framing claim grounded in staged capex and model-estimate sources
notes: Core essay argument; approve once supporting sources are promoted

claim: Frontier-model 50% time horizons are doubling roughly every 4-7 months, reaching ~5 hours of expert human task time by early 2026
caveat: Wide confidence intervals; benchmark tasks are cleaner than real work; 50% success is far below deployment reliability
notes: Upstream capability-layer claim only; never a country score

claim: AI capability is jagged across domains: agentic computer-use horizons are 40-100x shorter than software/reasoning horizons, and physical domains progress far slower
caveat: Domain coverage of benchmarks is partial
notes: Empirical anchor for the frontier-sensitivity axis of Figure 1

claim: A 50% time horizon does not imply an enterprise can safely delegate tasks of that length; economically valuable workflows demand >99% reliability
caveat: METR's own stated limitation
notes: Required caveat whenever time horizons appear in product copy

claim: The US-China gap in top AI model benchmark performance has effectively closed
caveat: Benchmark performance is not deployed capability; index methodology changes year to year

claim: US firms captured ~75% of 2025 global AI venture capital (~$194B) versus ~5% (~$13.9B) for China, implying divergent diffusion financing models
caveat: Staged source lacks primary OECD URL; VC location data has known attribution issues
notes: Promote primary source before public use

claim: Occupational exposure to generative AI is concentrated in high-skill, digitized, urban work, implying uneven distribution of early gains
caveat: Exposure is not displacement; realized effects depend on augmentation vs automation

claim: Frontier capability converts fastest where work is digital and feedback-rich (AI R&D, coding, cyber) and stalls where output depends on hardware, regulation, procurement, and trust (manufacturing, healthcare, public services)
caveat: Ordinal judgment synthesizing METR domain evidence and adoption patterns; Figure 1 placements are illustrative, not scored
notes: The central Atlas thesis; falsifiable via the signpost list in the launch essay

claim: If open-weight models compress the useful frontier gap, frontier sensitivity collapses as an axis and conversion capacity dominates outcomes
caveat: Scenario assumption, not a forecast; no probability estimated
notes: Feeds the scenario assumption browser
